content: A study investigating a different protozoan, Entamoeba histolytica, which produces similar symptoms, revealed that this organism secretes several neurologically active chemicals, including serotonin and Substance P. Elevated serum levels of serotonin have been observed in patients infected with Entamoeba histolytica. One paper highlighted that the diffuse symptoms associated with Blastocystis infection may correlate with serotonin's role in the body, suggesting that a similar mechanism could be involved in Blastocystis infections. Several reports have linked Blastocystis infection to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): A study conducted on IBS patients in the Middle East found that 46% of these patients were infected with Blastocystis, compared to only 7% of healthy controls. Another study in the Middle East demonstrated a significantly increased immune response to Blastocystis in IBS patients, even when the organism could not be detected in stool samples. A European study comparing Blastocystis infection rates in IBS patients versus healthy controls found a statistically significant higher infection rate in IBS patients. Early reports from U.S. physicians in the 1980s suggested that the presence of Blastocystis was not considered relevant to the diagnostic process, and patients infected with Blastocystis could still be diagnosed with IBS. Additionally, Blastocystis infection has been associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): A study that controlled for Blastocystis species identified subtypes 3 and 6 as the two subtypes responsible for producing intestinal inflammation. A case report described the coexistence of inflammatory bowel disease and Blastocystis infection. Experimental infection of mice with Blastocystis has been reported by three research groups to induce intestinal inflammation.
